Before class: set up your computer

Please do this at home or in your office. Conference Wi-Fi can be slow, and Task 01 needs the internet once.

  1. Install R 4.1.0 or newer from CRAN.
  2. Install RStudio Desktop from Posit's download page.
  3. Get the tutorial materials from github.com/XDai-bris/qtl2mr-tutorial: click Code → Download ZIP and unzip it, or run git clone https://github.com/XDai-bris/qtl2mr-tutorial.git.

MOTIVATION

Why Mendelian randomization in mice?

Suppose two traits move together in your Diversity Outbred (DO) cohort: mice with higher trait X also tend to have higher trait Y. Does X drive Y? We call the possible cause the exposure (X) and the trait it may affect the outcome (Y).

Some traits cannot simply be randomised in an experiment: you cannot assign a mouse its level of X the way you assign a diet. And a correlation alone does not answer the question, because two traits can move together for several reasons:

X → YX really changes Y: the effect we want to estimate.
Y → XReverse causation: Y changes X, and the arrow points the other way.
Shared causesCage, litter, diet or other loci move both traits (confounding).
A mixtureSeveral of these at once, which is common in real data.

Genetics as a natural experiment. At meiosis, each parent passes on one of its two alleles at random. Which allele a mouse inherits at a locus is therefore not chosen by its cage, litter or diet (relatedness between mice, such as littermates sharing alleles, is handled by the kinship matrix). If a QTL affects X, mice carrying different alleles there differ in X for reasons unrelated to those shared causes. If Y also differs between them, and the QTL affects Y only through X, that supports X → Y. This is the idea behind Mendelian randomization (MR).

Eight founders, not two alleles. DO mice descend from eight inbred founder strains, labelled A–H, so each chromosome is a mosaic of eight founder haplotypes. At one QTL there can be up to eight different allele effects, not just two. qtl2mr therefore uses the founder pattern at each QTL — the founder effects on X and on Y — rather than a single SNP.

What can go wrong. MR only works when the genetic instruments are valid. Most of today's diagnostics are about checking that, and about what to do when the checks raise doubts. All data in this workshop are simulated, so we know the true answer and can see when an analysis gets it right — and when a confident-looking answer is wrong.

HOW THIS GUIDE WORKS

One detailed workflow, then two extensions

MR uses genetic instruments — instrumental variables (IVs), here selected QTL — to investigate how an exposure X affects an outcome Y. A valid IV must predict X, be independent of confounders, and affect Y only through X. Today we learn what the estimates and diagnostics can tell us about these assumptions.

One of those diagnostics is Steiger filtering (SF): at each locus it compares how strongly the locus is associated with X and with Y, as a check on the direction X → Y. In this workshop SF is only reported and never used to remove instruments.

Single X–Y · Forward / ReverseRegional peaks → marginal F → MR → SF report
Case A · Three X traitsBatch analysis and observational comparison
Case B · Founder patternsSimilar slopes, different compatibility
Package exampleInstallation check only

What setup does

R/install.R checks that the bundled archive is the unchanged qtl2mr 0.6.0 release file, installs it into the project's private library/ folder, and checks its version and location. R/setup.R loads the workshop display helpers and creates a fresh results/run_… folder. The helpers format tables and plots; every package call that selects instruments or fits a model stays visible in the task code.

If told to restart R, restart and repeat Task 01. If a file cannot be found, open qtl2mr-tutorial.Rproj from the tutorial folder you downloaded or cloned. Installation messages can differ between computers.

TASK 02 · 10 MIN · 05–15

Meet one X–Y pair

Load 400 mice and identify the inputs before running MR.

Can an association arise through X → Y, or through Y → X? We have two simulated datasets on the same genetic base, called Forward and Reverse. We will analyse both as X → Y, then use diagnostics to question that interpretation.

show_table(data.frame(mouse_id=rownames(demo$covar)[1:4], head(demo$covar, 4)))
show_table(head(demo$marker_map, 4))

Pause and predict

Do the mixed colours directly measure heterozygosity?

Show an explanation

No. Marginal founder allele probabilities can reflect uncertainty and the two chromosome copies. Heterozygosity requires joint diplotype information. It is also different from the model parameter hsq.

Kinship, hsq and covariance are different quantities

K describes relatedness between mice. hsq is estimated under a covariate-only working variance model; it is not heterozygosity or the total genetic contribution of the simulation. ΣX and ΣY describe uncertainty of founder-effect estimates. ΣXY describes their cross-uncertainty, including shared samples. All 400 mice overlap here.

The single-pair base has correlated founder probabilities along each synthetic chromosome. A background relationship matrix R is constructed from chromosomes 13–19, with K = R/2. The phenotype innovations use covariance 0.1R + 0.3I. This teaching construction is not a full DO breeding simulation or a leave-one-chromosome-out kinship analysis; one kinship matrix is used at every locus.

How the two datasets were generated — return after Task 6
Forward: X = CαX + gS + ηX; Y = 0.9X + CαY + gL + ηY
Reverse: Y = CαY + gS + ηY; X = 0.9Y + CαX + gL + ηX

gS acts at nine source regions on chromosomes 1–9; gL acts at three additional regions on chromosomes 10–12. The genetic base, covariates and innovations are shared. In Forward the structural X-to-Y coefficient is 0.9; in Reverse it is zero. The Reverse source regions are associated with X through Y, while its local regions directly affect X.

Parameters, random seeds and noise were fixed before the first analysis and were not tuned afterwards. This contrast is an illustration, not a study of bias, coverage or direction-classification accuracy.

TASK 03 · 15 MIN · 15–30

From a scan to an IV set

See regional peak selection, then a separate marginal F check.

The exposure scan was run beforehand with qtl2, and we load its saved results. A LOD score (logarithm of the odds) summarizes the evidence that a marker is associated with X: the higher, the stronger. A region here is a contiguous run of markers with LOD ≥ 3; we take its highest marker.

3A · Find one peak in each region

R · Task 03A · same R session · tasks/03_selection.R
# PART A | From a scan to regional peaks
cat("\nTASK 03A | Many markers, one peak per region\n")
scan_forward <- readRDS("data/forward_scan.rds")
peaks_forward <- qtl2mr_select_instruments(
  resources_forward, scan_forward, exposures="x",
  lod_thresh=3, F_X_min=NULL, max_loci=NULL, progress=FALSE
)
cat("Markers scanned:", nrow(scan_forward), "| Candidate peaks:", nrow(peaks_forward), "\n")
show_table(head(peaks_forward[,c("marker","chr","pos","lod")],6))
plot_regional_selection(demo$marker_map, scan_forward, peaks_forward)
cat("Checkpoint: identify the highest marker in the shaded region.\n")

3B · Check marginal founder strength

Now apply the prespecified marginal founder F ≥ 4 gate. F measures how strongly the founder alleles at one locus, taken together, predict X; larger is stronger. This is a second decision, after regional peak selection.

R · Task 03B · same R session · tasks/03_selection.R
# PART B | Keep only peaks with adequate exposure strength
cat("\nTASK 03B | Apply the prespecified marginal F threshold\n")
instruments_forward <- qtl2mr_select_instruments(
  resources_forward, scan_forward, exposures="x",
  lod_thresh=3, F_X_min=4, max_loci=NULL, progress=FALSE
)
show_table(head(instruments_forward[,c("marker","lod","F_X_block","selected","drop_reason")],8))
cat("Retained:", sum(instruments_forward$selected),
    "| Rejected by F:", sum(instruments_forward$drop_reason=="F"), "\n")
plot_marginal_strength(instruments_forward)
cat("Milestone 3: regional peaks and the marginal F gate have produced the IV set.\n")

Pause and predict

Did SF remove the 34 rejected candidates?

Show an explanation

No. These candidates failed the prespecified marginal F gate. Steiger filtering (SF) has not been used for selection. In Task 6 it reports a statistic, and we explicitly choose a separate sensitivity IV set.

What these thresholds do — and do not — establish

The F statistic tests the founder-effect block at one locus, conditional on the covariates under the package working model. It is marginal across loci, not a conditional multi-locus F statistic. Four is a teaching threshold, not a universal definition of a strong or valid instrument; by default qtl2mr applies no F threshold.

Regional peak selection is not general LD-based clumping. Separate above-threshold islands can belong to one broad signal; selected regions are not automatically independent QTL. Here the final retained Forward loci are on three distinct chromosomes. LOD 3 was prespecified for this example and is not genome-wide significance calibration. Selecting and estimating in the same samples can introduce selection bias.

TASK 04 · 20 MIN · 30–50

Run Forward MR and inspect it

Read an estimate, its interval and its compatibility diagnostics.

4A · Fit the selected pair

The pair input connects X, Y and the three retained markers. Both traits are fitted at those same loci. Wait for the prompt to return before the next block.

R · Task 04A · same R session · tasks/04_forward.R
# PART A | Fit Forward once
cat("\nTASK 04A | Run Forward MR\n")
input_forward <- qtl2mr_pair_input(
  resources_forward, instruments_forward, exposure="x", outcome="y"
)
result_forward <- run_qtl2mr_analysis(
  input_forward, output_dir=file.path(run_dir,"forward"),
  standardize_phenotypes=FALSE, reported_estimator_policy="diagnostic_only",
  cross_cov_model="star", heterogeneity_method="chisq", diagnostic_bootstrap_B=0L,
  run_loo_mr=TRUE, run_instrument_sensitivity=FALSE,
  make_html=TRUE, make_figures=TRUE, verbose=FALSE, progress=FALSE
)
show_table(summary(result_forward)[,c("exposure","outcome","n_loci","estimate","ci_lower","ci_upper")])
plot_forward_result(result_forward)
Console output from the reference run
TASK 04A | Run Forward MR
 exposure outcome n_loci estimate ci_lower ci_upper
        x       y      3     0.88    0.765    0.994
Figure saved: figures/04_forward_mr.png

Read it aloud: “The estimated Y change per X unit is 0.880; the interval describes uncertainty under the fitted working model.” Three terms need a definition:

  • The working model is the simplified statistical model qtl2mr fits: a mixed model for each trait at each locus, and one common slope linking the founder effects on Y to those on X.
  • The profile interval is the range of slopes that this model finds compatible with the data at the 95% level.
  • It is nominal: it is computed as if the working model were exactly right, and its real coverage has not been checked. qtl2mr says so with inference_status = "not_calibrated".

A good-looking estimate is only the beginning.

4B · Check compatibility and influence

R · Task 04B · same R session · tasks/04_forward.R
# PART B | Read compatibility and influence
cat("\nTASK 04B | Read diagnostics with the estimate\n")
show_table(diagnostic_overview(result_forward))
loo_forward <- read_pair_table(result_forward,"loo_mr")
show_table(loo_forward[,c("marker","theta_minus_m","profile_ci_lower","profile_ci_upper")])
plot_forward_influence(result_forward,loo_forward)
cat("Milestone 4: I can read the estimate, interval, Q and leave-one-locus-out results.\n")
Console output from the reference run
TASK 04B | Read diagnostics with the estimate
 estimate lower upper      Q   Q_p warning
     0.88 0.765 0.994 10.007 0.968    none
     marker theta_minus_m profile_ci_lower profile_ci_upper
 chr01_m040         0.919            0.774            1.064

 chr02_m040         0.867            0.732            1.001
Figure saved: figures/05_forward_LOO.png 
Milestone 4: I can read the estimate, interval, Q and leave-one-locus-out results.

Q measures how far the founder effects on Y are from one common multiple of the founder effects on X, given their uncertainty. If every IV tells the same story, Q is about as large as its degrees of freedom (df) or smaller, so Q/df is around 1 or below; only values well above 1 flag incompatibility, also called heterogeneity. Here df = 7 founder contrasts × 3 loci − 1 = 20.

The global Q is 10.007 on 20 df (Q/df = 0.500; p = 0.968): this example does not show strong incompatibility with a common founder-effect slope. That does not establish IV validity. Read the leave-one-out estimates and intervals together.

What the settings and warnings mean

standardize_phenotypes = FALSE preserves phenotype units. cross_cov_model = "star" retains estimated within-locus X–Y cross-covariance. The primary profile interval is computed even though diagnostic_bootstrap_B = 0 skips the bootstrap for two comparison estimators. The chi-square Q reference is a working approximation.

run_instrument_sensitivity = FALSE prevents automatic subset refits, including a refit without the loci that fail Steiger filtering. The block-level direction statistics are still reported. primary_reliable describes numerical checks, not causal identification; inference_status = "not_calibrated" is not a coverage guarantee. Warnings must be read with the result. Several of these settings differ from the package defaults; see After the workshop.

Optional: the founder-pattern equation
r(θ) = βY − θβX
V(θ) = ΣY + θ²ΣX − θ(ΣXY + ΣXYᵀ)

The fit combines rᵀV⁻¹r across loci; Q is the smallest value of this sum. It asks whether the outcome founder effects resemble a common multiple of the exposure founder effects, accounting for uncertainty and within-locus overlap covariance. It does not account for every possible cross-locus dependence. The 95% profile interval contains the slopes whose sum is within 3.84 (the 95% point of a chi-square with 1 df) of Q. Confidence sets can be unbounded or disconnected; inspect their full representation in unfamiliar data.

Repeat on the Reverse dataset

Run the same analysis, then notice why a pooled slope is not enough.

TASK 05 | Repeat the workflow under Reverse
Candidate peaks: 51 | Retained: 5 
 estimate lower upper       Q    Q_p      warning
    0.843 0.726 1.017 188.196 <0.001 hsq_boundary
Figure saved: figures/06_forward_reverse_mr.png 
Milestone 5: Reverse also gives an MR estimate; its high Q needs explanation.

Notice the conflict: Reverse gives an estimate of 0.843 [0.726, 1.017], but Q is 188.196 on 34 df (Q/df = 5.535, p < 0.001). Its common-slope interpretation is strongly challenged. Keep the warning visible; Task 6 asks why.

Here the notice hsq_boundary (shown in the warning column) means that the estimated heritability of Y (hsq) is exactly 0, the edge of its allowed range, so the kinship term has no effect for Y. It is a model-fit note, not proof of reverse causation.

Why the Reverse output needs care

Reverse retains five candidates after F selection. Its selected source loci reflect Y → X; its additional X-local loci have a different relationship with Y. Pooling these mechanisms does not identify one valid X-to-Y effect. The nominal interval is not a valid confidence statement for the true X-to-Y coefficient under this violated model.

The outcome working-model hsq estimate is at zero, and the pipeline reports an hsq boundary warning. That is a variance-component fit diagnostic, not proof of reverse causation. We keep it alongside the high Q.

TASK 06 · 15 MIN · 55–70

Steiger filtering (SF): diagnose, then compare an IV set

Explain the five IVs, read partial R², and run one manual sensitivity analysis.

Keep the question fixed: X → Y. “Reverse” names the data-generating mechanism Y → X; it does not swap exposure and outcome in our analysis. Steiger filtering (SF) compares, at each locus, how strongly the locus is associated with X and with Y. A locus more strongly associated with Y than with X raises a question about the X → Y direction. In this workshop SF is only reported and never used to remove instruments; we decide whether a separate sensitivity analysis is informative.

0–3 minutes · Why three IVs become five

Forward data

Source regions → X → Y
Additional local regions → Y

Reverse data

Source regions → Y → X
Additional local regions → X

We scan X in both datasets, take one peak per above-threshold region (LOD ≥ 3), then require marginal F ≥ 4. In Reverse, X carries signals transmitted through Y and signals acting directly on X.

X scanCandidate regionsAfter F ≥ 4Retained regions
Forward373Chr1, Chr2, Chr3
Reverse515Chr1, Chr2, Chr3 + Chr10, Chr11

Five is the selection result, not an SF decision. The extra two retained regions affect X directly in this simulation. The counts are specific to this dataset; reverse causation does not always produce more IVs.

3–7 minutes · What does partial R² measure?

For each locus and each trait T (X or Y), ask: after accounting for covariates, how much of the remaining variation is associated with this founder block under the kinship working model? That share is the partial R².

R²T,ℓ = kFT,ℓ / (kFT,ℓ + νT)
Here: k = 7 founder contrasts; ν = 400 − 5 − 7 = 388 residual degrees of freedom.

F is the marginal founder F statistic from Task 3. Eight probabilities sum to one, leaving seven linearly independent contrasts. The five covariate columns include the intercept. For Forward Chr1, FX = 13.613 gives R²X = 0.197. This describes association after adjustment, not a causal effect or 19.7% of raw total phenotype variance.

R · Task 06A · same R session · tasks/06_direction.R
# PART A | Read the SF report and calculate one partial R-squared
cat("\nTASK 06A | SF compares associations; it does not remove IVs\n")
sf_forward <- read_pair_table(result_forward,"block_first_stage")
sf_reverse <- read_pair_table(result_reverse,"block_first_stage")
direction <- direction_table(sf_forward,sf_reverse)
show_table(direction)

# Here: 400 mice, 5 covariate columns including the intercept,
# and 7 independent founder contrasts: residual df = 400 - 5 - 7.
k <- 7
residual_df <- 400 - 5 - k
F_example <- sf_forward$F_X_block[sf_forward$marker == "chr01_m040"]
R2_example <- k * F_example / (k * F_example + residual_df)
show_table(data.frame(marker="chr01_m040",F_X=F_example,
                      k=k,residual_df=residual_df,R2_X=R2_example))
plot_direction(sf_forward,sf_reverse)

13–15 minutes · Say what we learned

Pause and predict

Did SF prove that Chr10 and Chr11 are valid, or that X has exactly zero effect?

Show an explanation

No. SF highlighted conflicting relative associations. Our explicit two-IV follow-up changes the estimate and weakens the evidence of pattern incompatibility; it does not prove IV validity, establish causal direction or prove a zero effect. Keep both results and explain the choice.

Milestone check: the Console confirms five IVs in the original analysis and two in the separate manual analysis, with automatic SF subset refit = FALSE for both. The original five-IV result is preserved.

Optional mathematics: F, adjusted variation and the working model
FT,ℓ = (β̂T,ℓᵀ Σ̂T,ℓ⁻¹ β̂T,ℓ) / k
R²T,ℓ = [RSSC − RSSC+Gℓ] / RSSC

β̂ is the k-dimensional founder-effect contrast vector; Σ̂ is its estimated covariance. The second formula is equivalent within the same fixed trait-specific whitening from the fitted kinship working model: RSS is the residual sum of squares of the whitened data, C is the covariate design, and Gℓ adds the founder block. It is not a ratio of degrees-of-freedom-adjusted variance estimates. X and Y have separately fitted working variance models. The values therefore summarize model-adjusted association, not raw total-variance fractions.

Here the full model rank is 12 (5 covariate columns + 7 contrasts), so ν = 388 for every displayed block. In another dataset, use the fitted ranks and residual degrees of freedom rather than copying 388. The Chr1 regional maximum also shifts from chr01_m040 in Forward to chr01_m038 in Reverse; these are the same source region, not identical marker sets plus two.

Interpretation limits and output field names

The package field steiger_pass is TRUE when R²X ≥ R²Y (including equality). We label this exposure-dominant, not “valid”. The comparison is a reported statistic, not a formal direction significance test. Measurement error, pleiotropy, ascertainment and sampling variation can alter its ordering. Do not automatically discard every Y-dominant locus or certify every X-dominant locus.

Both fits report hsq_boundary and inference_status = "not_calibrated". The displayed 95% profile intervals and chi-square Q p-values are nominal working-model outputs; the invalid five-IV pooled model does not provide valid causal coverage. The two-IV result is compatible with zero but does not demonstrate calibrated coverage or successful causal repair. This is not a formal nested Q-difference test.

run_instrument_sensitivity = FALSE disables the package's automatic subset refits. Our second run is a separate, explicit qtl2mr_pair_input() call. This lesson still fits X → Y twice; bidirectional MR would additionally select Y instruments and fit Y → X with its own assumptions.

Milestone 7: three separate univariable MR results, alongside observational estimates.

Read the contrast: MR is negative for X1, positive for X2 and compatible with zero for X3. All three observational intervals include zero. A point estimate's sign alone is not the conclusion.

How Case A was built. The observational slopes were deliberately built near zero (0.05, −0.05 and 0.02) through shared confounding: an unmeasured factor and background loci that affect both X and Y hide the real effects. MR lands near the specified values (−0.25, 0.25 and 0) because the instruments were built to act on Y only through X (apart from small local overlaps with the background terms; see below). With real data you cannot know this in advance.

Pause and predict

Are these three mutually adjusted causal effects?

Show an explanation

No. They are three separate univariable MR fits against the same Y, not a multivariable MR model. The X3 interval is compatible with zero; it does not prove an exactly zero effect.

Case A construction and the background coefficients
Xj = Cαj + gIV,j + 2Δj + ujU + kj + ej
YA = −0.25X1 + 0.25X2 + 0X3 + CαY + 0.7U + kY + eY
+ d1Δ1 + d2Δ2 + d3Δ3

The background effects were set by a single linear solve to produce the prespecified observational contrast. Each Δ combines twenty non-IV positions. The solve targeted observational slopes 0.05, −0.05 and 0.02, using the realized base outcome including its noise; it did not use MR estimates.

This deliberately constructed example is not a calibration experiment. Background terms retain local projections onto IV founder blocks. Case A uses normalized exponential founder-probability draws and a separately stipulated relationship matrix M with 100 four-mouse blocks, entries 0.3|i−j|, and K = M/2. It is a different genetic base from Forward/Reverse, not a DO meiosis or realistic LD simulation.

The observational intervals are descriptive covariate-adjusted ordinary least-squares intervals; they do not account for kinship or the targeting step. MR uses nominal profile intervals under its working assumptions.

Batch output and follow-up

Read status and warnings as well as effect estimates. The batch main-results file has one row per pair; locus output contains strength and direction statistics. This batch does not generate the full single-pair LOO and HTML report. Return to the single-pair interface for detailed follow-up. One worker is used on every platform in this lesson.

TASK 08 · 15 MIN · 85–100

Case B: why founder patterns matter

See how similar slopes can conceal different founder-effect patterns.

Case B is a small summary-effect example, not another 400-mouse dataset. It holds the exposure founder effects and their uncertainty fixed and changes the outcome founder pattern at one locus.

R · Task 08 · same R session · tasks/08_patterns.R
cat("\nTASK 08 | Case B: why founder patterns matter\n")
patterns <- readRDS("data/case_b_patterns.rds")
fit_proportional <- fit_multilocus_founder_mr(
  list(patterns$Proportional), allow_cross_cov=TRUE,
  compute_independence=FALSE, heterogeneity_method="chisq",q_sim_n=0L
)
fit_discordant <- fit_multilocus_founder_mr(
  list(patterns$Discordant), allow_cross_cov=TRUE,
  compute_independence=FALSE, heterogeneity_method="chisq",q_sim_n=0L
)
pattern_results <- compare_patterns(fit_proportional,fit_discordant)
show_table(pattern_results)
plot_patterns(patterns,fit_proportional,fit_discordant)
cat("Milestone 8: similar slopes can hide very different founder-pattern compatibility.\n")

TASK 08 | Case B: why founder patterns matter
      pattern estimate lower upper         Q    Q_p
 Proportional      0.5 0.451  0.55 9.361e-30      1
   Discordant    0.515 0.464 0.567   104.931 <0.001
Figure saved: figures/09_founder_patterns.png 
Milestone 8: similar slopes can hide very different founder-pattern compatibility.

Read the figure before the Q value: the proportional pattern follows one line. The discordant pattern departs from that line at selected founders. Its fitted slope remains near 0.5, but its Q is 104.931.

Why is the Proportional Q 9.361e-30 and not 0? By construction the outcome founder effects are exactly 0.5 × the exposure founder effects, so the best slope (0.5) leaves nothing unexplained and Q is exactly 0 in exact arithmetic. The tiny printed number is floating-point rounding noise; your computer may print a different tiny number, or 0.

Pause and predict

Does a discordant founder pattern prove horizontal pleiotropy (the locus affects Y through a path that bypasses X)?

Show an explanation

No. It demonstrates incompatibility with this common-slope model under the stated uncertainty. Pleiotropy is one possible explanation; data errors, model misspecification or other mechanisms can also produce incompatibility. A proportional direct effect may escape this diagnostic.

Pattern construction and what the residual bars mean

The centred exposure founder effects are (−2, −1.5, −1, −0.5, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2). The proportional outcome effects are 0.5 times these. The discordant version adds (0.5, −0.5, 0, 0, 0, 0, −0.5, 0.5). In the seven-dimensional contrast basis, ΣX = ΣY = 0.01I and ΣXY = 0.003I.

The teaching bars show H(βY − θβX) divided by the square root of the corresponding diagonal of HVHᵀ. These correlated founder residuals are not eight independent hypothesis tests and are not the package's native projected residual scores.

A single biallelic dosage projects the founder pattern onto one contrast. A multi-founder representation retains more of the pattern and can reveal incompatibility along other contrasts. This example illustrates information retained; it is not a head-to-head power benchmark or a claim that dosage-based approaches never detect heterogeneity.

MAIN ROUTE COMPLETE

Take-home messages

You have selected regional peaks, inspected founder strength, read direction reports and compared an explicitly chosen IV set, run a three-exposure batch and compared founder patterns.

  1. An estimate means little without its diagnostics. Read the interval, Q, leave-one-out results and the direction report together with the number.
  2. A confident-looking estimate can be wrong. Reverse gave 0.843 [0.726, 1.017] although the specified X-to-Y effect is zero.
  3. Q and SF flag problems but do not prove anything. They can point to invalid instruments, but they cannot tell you which explanation is right, or show that the instruments are valid.
  4. With real data there is no known true answer. Here the simulation told us the truth. In your own study, rely on design, choices made before seeing the results, and sensitivity analyses.

Installation needs helpFollow the reference outputs in this guide during the session and return to setup in the buffer time.

Pick up again after restarting R

Objects such as result_forward exist only in the running R session. After a restart, run Task 01 again — it reinstalls qtl2mr from package/ in a few seconds and starts a new results folder — then rerun, in order, the tasks before the one you want. Any task file can be run with source(). For example, to continue at Task 06:

R · resume after a restart
source("tasks/01_ready.R")
source("tasks/02_inputs.R")
source("tasks/03_selection.R")
source("tasks/04_forward.R")
source("tasks/05_reverse.R")
# ...then continue with Task 06

Tasks 07 and 08 need only Task 01. Task 06 needs Tasks 02–05. Task 09 needs Tasks 02–08.

Use qtl2mr in your own projects

The library/ folder belongs to this tutorial project only. For your own analyses, install the latest qtl2mr release from github.com/XDai-bris/qtl2mr-uvmr, following the installation steps in its README. Its vignettes — vignette("getting-started", package = "qtl2mr") and vignette("from-qtl2", package = "qtl2mr") — walk from a qtl2 cross to an analysis.

  1. Prepare aligned founder allele probabilities, phenotypes, covariates, kinship and map.
  2. Plan the exposure scan, regional selection and strength thresholds before examining MR results.
  3. Run one pair; read uncertainty, warnings, compatibility and direction statistics together.
  4. Expand to a batch, then return to individual pairs where diagnostics need investigation.

The workshop settings are chosen for speed and teaching

Some arguments in the task code differ from the qtl2mr 0.6.0 defaults, so that every task finishes in seconds and stays easy to read. With your own data, start from the defaults unless you have a reason to change them. Defaults can change in later releases, so check ?run_qtl2mr_analysis in the version you install.

ArgumentUsed inWorkshopPackage defaultWhat the default does
standardize_phenotypesTasks 04–07FALSETRUEFits both traits in standard-deviation units, so the effect is SD of Y per SD of X. The workshop keeps original units.
heterogeneity_methodTasks 04–06"chisq""auto"Chi-square p-value for one locus; for several loci, a p-value from 1,000 simulation draws (heterogeneity_nsim), which takes much longer. (In run_qtl2mr_batch() the default is already "chisq". Task 08 sets it too; for one locus "auto" is already chi-square.)
diagnostic_bootstrap_BTasks 04–060500Bootstrap draws for the weighted median and weighted mode comparison estimators. These are diagnostics, not the reported estimate. (In run_qtl2mr_batch() the default is already 0.)
run_instrument_sensitivityTasks 04–06FALSETRUERefits on standard subsets of instruments (the strongest loci, loci with F ≥ 2, one chromosome left out at a time, without the most influential loci) and runs the Steiger direction check described below.
lod_threshTasks 03, 0534LOD threshold for candidate regions in qtl2mr_select_instruments().
F_X_minTasks 03, 054NULLNo marginal F threshold: every candidate peak is kept, and F_X_block is still reported for each.
compute_independenceTask 08FALSETRUEfit_multilocus_founder_mr() also refits without the exposure–outcome cross-covariance, to show how much sample overlap moves the estimate.
verbose, progressTasks 03–07FALSETRUEPrints progress messages and, in run_qtl2mr_analysis(), a result summary (there the default progress = NULL follows verbose). Display only; the numbers do not change.

“SF never removes instruments” holds for this workshop. With the package defaults (run_instrument_sensitivity = TRUE), run_qtl2mr_analysis() also runs the Steiger direction check (the package's name for this SF refit): it repeats the fit without the loci whose partial R²X < partial R²Y and compares the result with the primary estimate in data/steiger_sensitivity.csv, adding a notice if the estimate moves outside the primary interval. This is a sensitivity analysis: the primary estimate still uses all instruments. run_qtl2mr_batch() does not run it; it flags those loci with steiger_pass in batch_locus_results.csv.

REFERENCE

Glossary

Mendelian randomization (MR)
A way to estimate the causal effect of an exposure on an outcome, using genetic variants as instruments. It relies on alleles being passed on at random at meiosis, and it is only as good as its instruments.
Exposure and outcome (X and Y)
The exposure X is the possible cause; the outcome Y is the trait it may affect. Every analysis in this workshop asks about X → Y.
Instrument, instrumental variable (IV)
A genetic locus used to make the MR comparison. A valid instrument (1) is associated with the exposure, (2) shares no causes with the outcome, and (3) affects the outcome only through the exposure. In qtl2mr each instrument is a selected QTL marker, represented by its founder allele probabilities.
QTL
Quantitative trait locus: a region of the genome where genetic differences are associated with differences in a trait.
Founder haplotype, founder effect
DO mice descend from eight inbred founder strains, labelled A–H. At each locus, each chromosome copy of a DO mouse comes from one founder; that stretch of chromosome is a founder haplotype. A founder effect is the estimated effect on a trait of carrying a given founder's haplotype at the locus. Because the eight founder probabilities sum to one, qtl2mr works with seven founder contrasts per locus.
Kinship (K)
A mouse-by-mouse matrix that says how closely related each pair of mice is. qtl2mr uses it in a linear mixed model so that related mice are not treated as independent. For your own data the package recommends one kinship matrix per chromosome, leaving that chromosome out (LOCO); this workshop supplies one matrix that is used at every locus.
LOD score
Logarithm of the odds: the log10 likelihood ratio of a model with an effect at the marker against a model without one. Higher values mean stronger evidence that the marker is associated with the trait. The workshop scans were run with qtl2.
F statistic (marginal founder F, F_X_block)
For one locus: the joint Wald statistic of its seven founder contrasts on the exposure, divided by 7 (F = β̂ᵀΣ̂⁻¹β̂ / 7). “Marginal” means one locus at a time, not adjusted for the other loci. Larger means a stronger instrument; F = 2 corresponds to nominal p ≈ 0.05. The workshop threshold F ≥ 4 is a teaching choice; by default qtl2mr applies no F threshold.
Profile interval
The 95% interval qtl2mr reports for the slope: all slopes whose objective is within 3.84 (the 95% point of a chi-square with 1 degree of freedom) of its minimum Q. With weak instruments it can be unbounded or split into pieces; then no finite interval is reported.
Q and Q/df (heterogeneity, compatibility)
Q is the minimum of the fit's objective: how far the founder effects on Y are from one common multiple of the founder effects on X, given their uncertainty. Its degrees of freedom are df = 7 × (number of loci) − 1. If all instruments agree, Q/df is around 1 or below; only values well above 1 flag incompatibility (heterogeneity). Q flags a problem but does not identify its cause, and a small Q does not prove that the instruments are valid.
Partial R²
The share of the variation left after the covariates (under the kinship working model) that is associated with a locus's founder block: R² = kF / (kF + ν), with k = 7 contrasts and ν residual degrees of freedom. Reported for X (R²X) and Y (R²Y) at every instrument.
Steiger filtering (SF)
A direction check that compares, at each locus, partial R²X with partial R²Y. qtl2mr reports steiger_pass = TRUE when R²X ≥ R²Y. In this workshop SF is only reported and never used to remove instruments. With the package defaults, qtl2mr also refits without the loci that fail, as a separate sensitivity analysis; the primary estimate keeps all instruments.
hsq and hsq_boundary
hsq is the heritability estimated for each trait (and, with per-chromosome kinship, each chromosome) from the kinship model with covariates but no locus, and then held fixed; it sets how much the kinship term matters in the mixed model. hsq_boundary is an information notice: an hsq estimate is on the edge of its range [0, 1]. At hsq = 0 the kinship term has no effect for that trait. It is not an error and not evidence about causal direction.
Nominal
Describes an interval or p-value computed from a formula that assumes the working model is right, such as the 95% chi-square cutoff. Whether it really covers the truth 95% of the time in a given situation has not been checked; qtl2mr reports inference_status = "not_calibrated".
Working model
The simplified statistical model qtl2mr fits: at each locus, a linear mixed model for each trait (covariates, founder effects and a kinship term with fixed hsq), and one common slope θ linking the founder effects on Y to those on X. Results are statements under this model; when it is wrong, for example with invalid instruments, its intervals and p-values can mislead.
